options.A: Neonatal tetanus infection
options.B: An acute allergic reaction to breastmilk
options.C: Normal physiological jaundice
options.D: Severe congenital heart disease

explanation: You're learning fast! Mild yellowing around day two or three is usually normal physiological jaundice as the baby's young liver processes extra red blood cells.

question: Which landmark appears as a vertical streak running across the upper portion of the normal tympanic membrane?

options.A: The annular ligament ring
options.B: The incus bone joint
options.C: The Eustachian tube opening
options.D: The handle of the malleus

explanation: The handle of the malleus is embedded in the eardrum and shows clearly as a streak extending down from the top edge. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h6)

question: According to modern safety science, why do healthcare errors usually happen?

options.A: They are entirely unpredictable acts of bad luck
options.B: They are caused by faulty systems and poor work conditions
options.C: They happen because nurses simply do not care enough
options.D: They only occur when doctors fail to write clear orders

explanation: Spot on! Modern safety science reminds us that errors usually stem from flawed work environments, not just individual carelessness. You're learning fast!

question: What is the maximum expected duration for normal postpartum blues before they should resolve?

options.A: Forty-eight hours
options.B: One year
options.C: Six months
options.D: Two weeks

explanation: Postpartum blues typically peak around the fourth or fifth day and resolve spontaneously within the first two weeks after delivery. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T010#GNS226_U1_T010_h6)

question: Why does pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) raise a woman's risk of having an ectopic pregnancy?

options.A: Hormonal imbalances stop the uterine lining from growing
options.B: Scar tissue blocks and damages the fallopian tubes
options.C: Infection prevents the ovaries from releasing eggs
options.D: Bacteria destroy the muscular walls of the uterus

explanation: When PID heals, it leaves behind scar tissue that narrows the tubes. If a fertilized egg gets stuck in that narrow, scarred tube, it implants right there instead of the uterus.

question: What usually happens if a patient's thinking part of the brain is badly damaged, but their brainstem is totally fine?

options.A: The patient loses awareness of the environment but may still sleep and wake
options.B: The patient loses all reflex actions while keeping clear thoughts
options.C: The patient stays completely awake but loses the ability to feel pain
options.D: The patient enters an immediate state of permanent brain death

explanation: You're doing great! Because the brainstem handles sleep-wake cycles, an undamaged brainstem means the body can still cycle between sleeping and waking up, even without higher thinking.

question: Why can it be so tricky to spot a drug side effect in someone with a degenerative disease?

options.A: Patients with degenerative illnesses never tell anyone how they feel
options.B: Lab tests can never detect drug levels in chronic illnesses
options.C: Drug side effects always cause a sudden skin rash
options.D: Side effects like tremors or confusion can easily look like the disease getting worse

explanation: You're doing great! It's a classic clinical puzzle: if a drug causes shakiness or confusion, it's easy to assume the disease is simply progressing, when the patient might actually just need a medication adjustment.

question: What is the most important thing to look at when choosing a research design?

options.A: The nature of the research question
options.B: The color of the hospital ward walls
options.C: The personal hobby of the lead nurse
options.D: The brand of computer in the office

explanation: Spot on! Your research question is the boss—it tells you whether you need an experiment, a survey, or an interview study.

question: Why do doctors test breast cancer tissue for HER2 receptors?

options.A: It tells the doctor exactly how many months the patient has to live
options.B: It prevents the cancer from spreading to the bone marrow
options.C: It proves the patient has a family history of endocrine disorders
options.D: It identifies tumors that may respond to specific HER2-blocking medications

explanation: Finding HER2 helps doctors target the cancer directly with specialized medications that block these specific growth signals. Modern medicine is amazing like that! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h4)

question: How do strong cultural preferences for traditional birth attendants usually affect postnatal referrals?

options.A: They ensure all newborn red flags are diagnosed early
options.B: They often cause dangerous delays in seeking formal medical care
options.C: They train primary health nurses in advanced surgical skills
options.D: They help finance hospital transport for emergency cases

explanation: When families trust traditional options first, it can delay them from coming to the clinic until complications become life-threatening.

question: Approximately how many extra calories does an exclusively breastfeeding mother need each day?

options.A: 100 to 200 calories
options.B: 450 to 500 calories
options.C: 800 to 1000 calories
options.D: No extra calories are needed

explanation: Making breast milk takes a lot of energy, requiring about 450 to 500 extra calories daily for an exclusively nursing mother. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h2)

question: Why are auto-disable syringes specifically used during routine immunization campaigns?

options.A: They lock automatically after one use to prevent accidental reuse
options.B: They allow nurses to draw medication much faster than regular needles
options.C: They can be safely disposed of in regular household waste bins
options.D: They reduce the physical pain of the injection for crying infants

explanation: Auto-disable syringes are designed to render themselves unserviceable after a single injection, stopping the spread of infections from reused equipment. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h6)

question: Where inside a liver cell do you mostly find the famous Cytochrome P450 enzymes?

options.A: Nucleus of red blood cells
options.B: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum of liver cells
options.C: Cell membrane of skeletal muscle tissue
options.D: Mitochondria of the brain

explanation: These hardworking CYP450 enzymes hang out densely packed in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of liver cells (hepatocytes). They do the heavy lifting of drug breakdown!

question: What is the main feature of a correlational study?

options.A: Variables are not manipulated by the researcher
options.B: Random assignment is used for all participants
options.C: A specific medication is tested on patients
options.D: Only laboratory animals are studied

explanation: Spot on! In correlational studies, we simply observe natural relationships without changing or controlling things ourselves. You've got this!

question: Why is a pressure bandage placed on the arm right after an implant procedure?

options.A: To keep the arm completely paralyzed for two weeks
options.B: To prevent the hormone from leaking into the air
options.C: To push the implant deep down into the bone marrow
options.D: To minimize bruising and swelling at the site

explanation: The pressure bandage acts as a gentle hug for the insertion site during the first 24 hours, keeping swelling and bruising down to a minimum.

question: What is the common medical name for the external female reproductive organs?

options.A: The vestibule
options.B: The vulva
options.C: The introitus
options.D: The perineum

explanation: You've got this! The entire external female genital area is known medically as the vulva. It's a handy term to remember for your clinical rotations.

question: Which nursing action helps prevent joint stiffness (contractures) in a patient on bed rest?

options.A: Restricting fluid intake to reduce swelling
options.B: Keeping the bed locked in a flat position all day
options.C: Performing range-of-motion exercises regularly
options.D: Applying ice packs to every major joint

explanation: Moving joints gently through their full range keeps muscles and tendons flexible and stops them from tightening up permanently.

question: How do long-term high food prices contribute to chronic illnesses like diabetes and obesity in vulnerable communities?

options.A: By eliminating the body's natural ability to process natural sugars
options.B: By forcing families to rely heavily on cheap, highly processed, carbohydrate-heavy foods
options.C: By providing extra financial funds for families to buy excessive amounts of meat
options.D: By encouraging children to exercise less due to high grocery store bills

explanation: When healthy food becomes too expensive, families buy cheap processed items that lack nutrition and promote chronic disease. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T026#GNS227_U2_T026_h8)

question: What happens when a person suffers severe damage to their hippocampus?

options.A: They lose the ability to feel physical pain
options.B: They experience paralysis in their lower limbs
options.C: They forget all their childhood memories
options.D: They can no longer form new long-term memories

explanation: You nailed it! The hippocampus is needed to lock in new experiences into long-term storage, so damage makes forming new memories very difficult.

question: Which of these personal items must kitchen staff take off before they start working?

options.A: Non-slip kitchen shoes
options.B: Hairnets and caps
options.C: Clean cotton aprons
options.D: Rings and wristwatches

explanation: Rings and watches trap dirt and hidden bacteria that are tough to wash away. Taking them off keeps the kitchen truly clean!

question: What might happen if a poor metabolizer takes a prodrug that relies on enzymes to become active?

options.A: The drug may fail to produce the desired therapeutic effect
options.B: The drug converts instantly and causes severe acute toxicity
options.C: The liver permanently stores the drug in fatty tissues
options.D: The kidneys immediately flush the drug out unchanged

explanation: That's right! Prodrugs need liver enzymes to wake them up and make them active. If those enzymes are too slow, the drug won't work like it should. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T5#GNS125_U1_T5_h3)

question: What do anticoagulant medications actually do in the body?

options.A: Make the circulating blood thicker
options.B: Dissolve existing blood clots completely
options.C: Stop platelets from clumping together
options.D: Prevent the formation of new blood clots

explanation: Think of anticoagulants as your body's stop sign for new clots. They don't break down clots that are already there, but they stop new ones from forming or getting bigger!

question: What is the main role of the family when supporting someone with a long-term condition like HIV?

options.A: Taking over all medical prescription duties
options.B: Isolating the patient from community stressors
options.C: Replacing the clinical healthcare team entirely
options.D: Acting as vital partners in the care continuum

explanation: You've got this! Families don't replace doctors or nurses; instead, they walk right beside the healthcare team to support the patient's long-term health journey.

question: What is the correct gap to keep between the top of the crutch and the patient's armpit?

options.A: Exactly one full hand width
options.B: Five to six finger widths
options.C: Two to three finger widths
options.D: No gap, it should touch firmly

explanation: A 2 to 3 finger-width gap keeps the crutch from pressing into the armpit nerves while the patient walks.

question: What is the primary purpose of public health surveillance systems during an infectious disease threat?

options.A: To calculate the annual financial profits of private clinics
options.B: To punish hospitals that fail to meet administrative standards
options.C: To restrict all international trade between neighboring nations
options.D: To detect, track, and report unusual disease outbreaks quickly

explanation: Surveillance monitors disease patterns so health agencies can spot outbreaks early and take action to protect the public. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h9)

question: A nurse is caring for a patient with acute glomerulonephritis. Which nursing action is most critical during the acute phase?

options.A: Providing a high-protein diet to rebuild lost muscle
options.B: Massaging swollen legs to improve local circulation
options.C: Accurately measuring every intake and output volume
options.D: Encouraging high fluid intake by offering extra water

explanation: Tracking every drop that goes in and comes out (I&O) is essential to monitor failing kidney function and catch dangerous fluid buildup early.

question: What is a major risk for a hospitalized patient who stays in a severe negative energy balance for too long?

options.A: Excessive fluid retention in lower extremities
options.B: Elevated resting metabolic rate above normal limits
options.C: Rapid increase in subcutaneous fat stores
options.D: Lean muscle wasting and delayed wound healing

explanation: When patients don't get enough calories, their bodies start breaking down muscle for fuel, making it hard for wounds to heal. Nutrition is vital care!

question: Which of these is a great example of a non-verbal communication cue during a patient interaction?

options.A: Body posture and facial expressions
options.B: Medical jargon used in charting
options.C: The specific tone of spoken words
options.D: A written discharge instruction

explanation: Correct! Non-verbal communication is all about body language—like a reassuring smile, a nod, or how someone sits. It often speaks louder than words!

question: What usually happens to a patient when their pancreas stops making enough digestive enzymes?

options.A: Malabsorption and nutritional deficiencies
options.B: Severe dehydration from excessive water retention
options.C: Widespread hardening of the intestinal walls
options.D: Rapid weight gain due to unchecked fat storage

explanation: Without enough enzymes, food passes through without being properly broken down, meaning the body misses out on vital nutrients and vitamins. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h7)

question: Why is a fever in a neutropenic patient considered a medical emergency?

options.A: It causes severe bleeding that is impossible to stop
options.B: A compromised immune system means a mild infection can rapidly turn fatal
options.C: It always causes permanent paralysis in the legs
options.D: It instantly stops the kidneys from producing any urine

explanation: Without enough white blood cells to fight back, a small fever can quickly become overwhelming. Quick action with antibiotics saves lives here!

question: What is a major advantage that barrier methods like condoms have over hormonal methods?

options.A: They never need to be replaced or bought again
options.B: Protection against sexually transmitted infections
options.C: They require no active participation during intercourse
options.D: They completely stop menstrual bleeding forever

explanation: Spot on! While hormonal methods prevent pregnancy, only barrier methods like condoms give that dual protection against STIs as well.

question: Why can prolonged isolation during a hospital stay negatively impact physical recovery?

options.A: Loneliness and lack of social support can worsen stress and delay healing
options.B: Patients without visitors automatically stop taking prescribed drugs
options.C: Social isolation directly causes elevated blood glucose levels
options.D: Isolation increases the body's need for intravenous fluids

explanation: Psychosocial distress triggers physiological stress responses that can weaken immunity and slow down recovery times. [learn more](GNS112_U1_T4#GNS112_U1_T4_h5)

question: During an abdominal check, how do midwives usually measure how far the baby's head has moved down?

options.A: In centimetres of cervical dilation
options.B: In fifths palpable above the pubic bone
options.C: By the station of the ischial spines
options.D: By the volume of amniotic fluid leaked

explanation: You're doing great! By feeling the abdomen, we estimate how many 'fifths' of the baby's head can still be felt above the pubic bone to track descent.

question: What is the medical term for the hard lumps of uric acid crystals that form under the skin in long-term gout?

options.A: Tophi
options.B: Vesicles
options.C: Pustules
options.D: Nodes

explanation: Remember: Tophi are solid bumps of urate crystals that can build up under the skin and around joints when gout isn't well controlled over time.

question: Which ethical principle gives a patient the right to make their own informed choices about treatment?

options.A: Paternalism
options.B: Autonomy
options.C: Maleficence
options.D: Beneficence

explanation: Autonomy means self-reliance and giving individuals the moral right to decide what happens to their own bodies. Keep building that nursing knowledge!

question: What is a major challenge nurses often face when providing palliative care in resource-limited settings?

options.A: An excess of high-tech equipment that overwhelms patients
options.B: Limited access to essential pain medications and specialized facilities
options.C: A complete absence of family involvement in patient care
options.D: Patients refusing all forms of basic nursing assessment

explanation: In many resource-constrained settings, getting a steady supply of pain relief like opioids can be tough. Nigerian nurses often have to be creative and strong advocates for their patients!

question: What is the main goal when giving culturally sensitive nutrition counseling?

options.A: To eliminate all traditional cooking methods from the community
options.B: To adapt healthy eating advice to fit the patient's local lifestyle and foods
options.C: To replace all local food items with expensive imported supplements
options.D: To force every patient to adopt a westernized diet style

explanation: Good nursing care works with what the patient already eats and enjoys, making healthy lifestyle changes realistic and sustainable.

question: A patient has a critically high potassium level. Which emergency medication combo helps push potassium out of the blood and back into the cells?

options.A: Aspirin and intravenous heparin
options.B: Furosemide and oral iron tablets
options.C: Normal saline and potassium chloride
options.D: Regular insulin and glucose

explanation: Brilliant! Insulin acts like a key to drive potassium safely back inside the cells, while glucose is given right along with it to keep the blood sugar stable.

question: How does general palliative care differ from standard hospice care?

options.A: Palliative care is only provided in outpatient clinics, while hospice care is strictly for hospital inpatients.
options.B: Palliative care can be given alongside curative treatments, whereas hospice care begins when curative treatment has stopped.
options.C: Palliative care is managed entirely by physicians, whereas hospice care is run strictly by volunteers.
options.D: Palliative care focuses exclusively on spiritual counseling, while hospice care manages physical pain.

explanation: You nailed it! Think of hospice as a specific type of palliative care reserved for the final phase of life, while general palliative care can start on day one.

question: What kind of skin do you usually see in someone with untreated hypothyroidism?

options.A: Flushing and oily patches
options.B: Warm, moist, and smooth skin
options.C: Bronze hyperpigmentation
options.D: Dry, coarse, and cold skin

explanation: A slow metabolism means the sweat and oil glands aren't working at full speed, leaving the skin feeling dry, rough, and chilly.

question: What exactly is metabolism?

options.A: The rate at which the heart pumps blood to tissues
options.B: The total amount of water lost through skin and urine
options.C: All the chemical reactions that occur within the body
options.D: The physical process of digesting food in the stomach

explanation: Think of metabolism as the master umbrella for every chemical process happening in your cells to keep you alive and kicking. You've got this!
